w: At 267,954 hectares, this is the most central of eight protected areas forming the UNESCO Greater Blue Mountains Area, listed in 2000. An uplifted, dissected plateau rather than true mountains, it climbs from 20 metres on the Nepean River to 1,215 metres at Mount Werong. Its walking tracks are heritage-listed.

The only mountain in the Jamison Valley, a few kilometres south of Katoomba, which is how it earned its English name; the local Aboriginal name is Korowal, meaning 'the strong one'. Part of the Blue Mountains Range within Blue Mountains National Park, roughly 100 kilometres west of Sydney.
s: Only mountain in the Jamison Valley
_facts: Local name Korowal, meaning 'the strong one'
Only peak in the Jamison Valley
A few km south of Katoomba

w: Known locally by its Aboriginal name Wirindi, this Explorer Range summit south of Mount Victoria is the trailhead for bushwalks down to caves, rock-climbing crags and the valley floor. Views over the Kanimbla Valley are softened by eucalypt cover, but it remains a popular launch point for a day on the escarpment.
s: Trailhead to caves and rock-climbing crags
_facts: Reached via a loop road from Mount Victoria
Bushwalk trailhead to caves and climbing areas

w: A 28-hectare cool-climate garden at Mount Tomah, on the boundary of the UNESCO Greater Blue Mountains Area, about 100 kilometres from Sydney via the Bells Line of Road. Originally the Mount Tomah Botanical Garden, it is heritage-listed and high enough to grow species that struggle in the Sydney basin.
s: Cool-climate garden on the World Heritage line
_facts: Formerly the Mount Tomah Botanical Garden
Reached via the Bells Line of Road
On the Greater Blue Mountains World Heritage boundary

w: The Casino dome atop this clifftop hotel was bought in Chicago, shipped to Australia, then hauled the last leg to Medlow Bath by bullock train and reassembled on site. The result is a heritage-listed jumble of Art Deco and Edwardian styles overlooking the Megalong Valley from the Great Western Highway.
s: A Chicago dome hauled in by bullock train
_facts: Art Deco and Edwardian architectural mix

w: Saved from logging by early Australian conservationists, this stand of blue gums in the Grose Valley is now one of the country's best-known bushwalking destinations. It sits within Blue Mountains National Park and the UNESCO-listed Greater Blue Mountains Area, reached on foot down into the valley floor.
s: Forest saved from the axe by conservationists
_facts: Grose Valley, Blue Mountains National Park
Saved from logging by early conservationists
Within the Greater Blue Mountains World Heritage Area

w: Norman Lindsay's stone cottage and studios at Faulconbridge, built 1898 to 1913 by the artist and his wife Rose, still stand on 17 hectares of former farmlet. Now a National Trust gallery and museum, the property doubled as the film set for 1994's Sirens, based on Lindsay's life and work.
s: Artist Norman Lindsay's cottage and studios
_facts: Owned by the National Trust of Australia

w: Ken Beames built this observatory and optical-instrument workshop by hand between 1938 and 1948, manufacturing precision components as K Beames Engineering Co. Now run by the Linden Observatory Trust, the heritage-listed site doubles as museum, education facility and meeting venue.
_facts: Also known as K Beames Engineering Co
Now doubles as museum and education facility

w: A rock shelter in the Blue Labyrinth section of Blue Mountains National Park, within walking distance of the town of Glenbrook, preserves Australian Aboriginal rock art. It ranks among the more accessible Indigenous heritage sites in the greater Blue Mountains, reachable without a full bushwalking expedition.
_facts: In the Blue Labyrinth area of Blue Mountains National Park
Rock shelter with Aboriginal rock art

w: The Nepean River spills out of a Hawkesbury sandstone gorge here to form a broad basin near Wallacia, long used as a swimming hole. It is the only picnic area on this stretch of the Nepean and one of the most popular water-based picnic spots in Greater Western Sydney, with camping and an education centre.
s: River swimming hole out of a sandstone gorge
_facts: Formed by the Nepean River exiting a sandstone gorge
Only picnic area on this stretch of the Nepean

w: This railway outpost swelled past 5,000 residents by 1908, almost all of them navvies building the Ten Tunnels Deviation, when it served as the works' headquarters. The deviation opened in 1910, a new platform was built on the realigned line, and the boomtown emptied out almost as fast as it had filled.
s: Boomtown built for the Ten Tunnels Deviation
_facts: Headquarters for the Ten Tunnels Deviation works by 1908

w: A wildlife park with its own dolphinarium operated near Warragamba from 17 August 1968 until 1991, a safari-style attraction on Sydney's western fringe near the Blue Mountains foothills. It has since closed, one of several vanished mid-century tourist ventures that once dotted the approach to the range.
s: Defunct safari park with its own dolphinarium
